name: Reginald Whitlock
presenting_complaint: Acutely confused and agitated overnight on the ward, pulling at IV lines

medications: Oxycodone 5 mg PRN (started day 2 for back pain)
medical_history.social: Lives with wife, independent with walking frame at baseline, no cognitive concerns before admission. Ex-smoker. Minimal alcohol.

validation_criteria.presenting_scenario: A 78-year-old man with Parkinson's disease, day 3 of an admission for a mechanical fall, becomes acutely confused and agitated overnight. Nursing report he is fluctuating between drowsy and agitated, pulling at his IV cannula, disoriented to place and time, and cannot sustain attention. His wife says he was cognitively normal at baseline. Obs: temp 37.9, HR 98, RR 22, SpO2 93% on room air, BP 148/86, GCS 14. He has not passed urine for 10 hours and his oxycodone was increased yesterday.
validation_criteria.task: Document your assessment and initial management as the admitting RMO.

subjective: Establish this is an ACUTE, FLUCTUATING change from baseline with inattention — i.e. delirium, not dementia (baseline cognition normal per wife)
Obtain COLLATERAL history from wife/nursing/notes: baseline cognition, function, onset and course of confusion (single most important step)

Medication review as a cause: recently increased opioid (oxycodone), anticholinergic burden, benzodiazepines, steroids; and check Parkinson's medication has NOT been missed/withheld (dopaminergic withdrawal precipitates delirium and NMS-like states)

Screen for reversible precipitants by symptom: fever/dysuria (infection), pain, constipation, urinary retention (no urine 10 hours + BPH + tamsulosin), poor oral intake/dehydration, alcohol/benzo withdrawal history
Document allergies and current medication list including PRN administrations overnight
objective: Formal delirium screen with a validated tool: 4AT or CAM (confirms inattention + acute fluctuating course)
Full set of observations including temperature and SpO2; targeted infection exam — chest, urine, skin, IV line sites
Palpate/bladder-scan for URINARY RETENTION (post-void residual) given BPH, tamsulosin and 10 hours without voiding
Focused neurological exam for focal signs/head injury (recent fall, ?anticoagulant) to decide on CT brain
Bedside tests: BGL, ECG (rate/rhythm, QTc before any sedation), review fluid balance and bowel chart (constipation)
assessment: Delirium (acute confusional state) — hyperactive/mixed — in an elderly man with Parkinson's disease, precipitated by an identifiable organic cause (document AS DELIRIUM, not 'dementia')
Likely precipitants: infection (?UTI/chest, temp 37.9, SpO2 93%), urinary retention, recently increased opioid, and pain — screen and treat each
Consider Lewy body/Parkinson's disease dementia as a vulnerability factor conferring severe neuroleptic sensitivity — this shapes drug safety
Differentials to exclude: hypoxia, sepsis, metabolic derangement, intracranial event post-fall, dopaminergic (Parkinson's medication) withdrawal
plan: Get collateral history and confirm baseline (FIRST action), then complete 4AT/CAM and document delirium diagnosis

Cause screen (DIMTOP): Drugs (deprescribe/reduce opioid, avoid anticholinergics, ensure Parkinson's meds given on time), Infection (FBC, CRP, urinalysis + MSU, CXR, blood cultures if septic), Metabolic (UEC, calcium, magnesium, LFT, TFT, BGL, B12/folate), Oxygen/hypoxia (SpO2, ABG if indicated), Trauma/intracranial (CT brain if focal signs, anticoagulated, head injury or no cause found), Pain/retention/constipation (bladder scan +/- catheter for retention, bowel chart, laxatives)

NON-PHARMACOLOGICAL first-line: reorientate (clock, calendar, familiar faces/wife present), glasses and hearing aids, quiet well-lit room, normalise sleep-wake cycle, avoid ward moves, mobilise, hydrate, remove unnecessary lines/catheters once retention excluded, treat pain adequately

Targeted treatment of the reversible cause: e.g. treat infection per local guideline, relieve urinary retention (bladder scan then catheterise if retained), correct hypoxia/electrolytes, manage constipation, review and minimise culprit drugs
Ensure Parkinson's medication continues on schedule via the correct route (NG/rotigotine patch if nil-by-mouth) — do NOT omit levodopa

ONLY if there is risk of harm to self/others AND non-drug de-escalation has failed, use lowest effective dose on senior advice: in Parkinson's/Lewy body disease AVOID typical/most atypical antipsychotics — cautious low-dose quetiapine 12.5-25 mg PO (Parkinson's-safe option) or a low-dose short-acting benzodiazepine (e.g. lorazepam 0.5 mg) is preferred; monitor obs, sedation and QTc
Escalate to senior/medical team and geriatrics; document diagnosis as delirium with cause, plan for reassessment and family communication

critical_errors: Giving an antipsychotic (e.g. haloperidol, olanzapine, risperidone) to sedate this patient with Parkinson's disease / possible Lewy body dementia — can precipitate severe neuroleptic sensitivity, marked rigidity and life-threatening deterioration
Mislabelling the presentation as 'dementia' in the notes instead of documenting DELIRIUM with a cause screen, so the reversible organic precipitant is missed
Omitting or withholding the patient's regular Parkinson's (levodopa) medication, which itself precipitates delirium and a neuroleptic-malignant-like syndrome
Sedating first without searching for and treating the reversible cause (e.g. missed urinary retention, opioid toxicity, infection, hypoxia)
must_not_miss: A reversible/organic precipitant identified and treated (urinary retention, infection, hypoxia, opioid/medication) — delirium is a medical emergency, not a nuisance
Urinary retention excluded with a bladder scan (10 hours no void, BPH, tamsulosin)
Intracranial event considered after the recent fall (CT brain if focal signs/anticoagulated/no cause found)
Delirium screened with a validated tool (4AT/CAM) and documented AS delirium, not dementia
